dispositions.upstream: Adopt upstream byte-bounded, Unicode-safe thread reads while retaining handoff-aware recent runs, round-specific result acknowledgements and fork task admission. Result acknowledgement uses the bounded returned items, so truncated results remain unread.
requirements: A read-only agent may delegate only read-only roles, in its own environment. A worker may hold a watch as a lead does, and its result waits for it; automatic landing and Forge watches still wake the owning parent. A configured role policy requires every new `delegate_task` child to be managed; `offPolicyReason` cannot bypass it. Without a configured policy, raw delegation remains available; accepted requests remain replayable. `delegate_task`/`followup` flows: any managed task can be followed up; the thread that owns a running managed task may also steer or queue to its child thread, while another thread is refused and a finished task continues through `followup`; advisors are reused and wait for published results; pinned read-only helpers share the lead's workspace but serialize with isolated writers; isolated writers validate their workspace at launch and hand back a revision; delegation to any registered project including No project chats; delegation skips models whose accounts are out of usage; idle advisors close per setting; a managed task's browser tabs close when it ends; agents can read their thread's terminal; default child permission level is a setting; a managed role runs with exactly its resolved options, never the delegating thread's own, and discovery and dispatch agree on them (a refusal names every offending option, review field or changed account; options the caller merely echoes from its own thread for the same account and model, such as `fastMode`, that the role does not set are dropped rather than refused, and the refusal names an account with allowance, not a usage-limited one); pending background work holds a thread's completion (it reads Waiting, not Ready) until it ends or is stopped; a managed task, or a child identified by subagent lineage without a managed binding, holds its result for an awaited command or monitor only through a 15-minute grace after the run that produced it ended — the original task and each follow-up judged by its own result run — then publishes it naming that work abandoned, while a command it did not await never holds it and its subagents, opaque background tasks and watches always do; a Stop writes an event only when it changes something, so a repeated Stop on a settled thread writes none.

dispositions.upstream: Adopt stopped worktree-setup queuing, overlapping checkpoint/turn-start reservations and canonical checkout identity; retain owned-workspace recovery guards, Jujutsu status and allocation intent ownership.
requirements: Jujutsu VCS driver (status, diff, files, per-turn checkpoints, restore), whose branch read is the project's integration bookmark answered by the driver rather than a Git command that fails in a checkout without `.git`, and which never reaches a thread's branch (only a Git checkout syncs one); jj repositories detected, including colocated checkouts and repositories whose checkout predates `slipjay.json`; repository detection stops at the nearest `.git` or `.jj`; new threads get an automatic workspace except explicit project-checkout launches; a launch with a Forge item (`buildItem`) resumes that item's workspace or creates one attached to it, before the agent starts; a thread whose workspace SlipJay removed (landed, or idle with no unlanded work) gets a fresh workspace on its next message or terminal open, which takes its Forge item (linked, or the one its workspace was attached to) only when no other workspace holds it, so it never joins another thread's checkout, and a turn and a terminal recovering it together keep the one checkout the thread is bound to, its agent is told on the first turn in the new workspace, which it calls fresh only when SlipJay's receipt says it created the checkout (a workspace it resumed is called resumed, and one with no receipt unconfirmed), and when no replacement can be allocated the turn runs on the project checkout instead of failing, with the thread bound there and its agent told to allocate a workspace before changing files, the thread keeps its Forge item through any replacement, even a failed one or one that could not take the item, and the agent is told why, and the thread keeps its strip after the removal, while a delegated task's removed workspace is deliberately not replaced (it belongs to the work that assigned it, so its turn fails as Workspace missing and says so) and a branch-bound thread's managed worktree is recreated from its branch, failing as Workspace missing when it cannot be; a launch never removes a resumed workspace on cancel; a thread can move workspaces, and the turn the move detaches leaves none of its tool calls open (a run that ends without a provider terminal, by detach or stream failure, interrupts its open items with it, while a normal terminal still leaves background commands running), so the thread never sits on Waiting for a dead call; Codex sandboxed writers, `isolated`-assigned, can write the repository store their workspace shares and one temp directory of their own, given to their own thread's shell as `TMPDIR` rather than the app-server's environment (every task on a session shares that), made for the task's turn and removed when it ends, or with the thread or server, so two tasks never share or inherit one; SlipJay errors keep their cause, and a failed `slipjay` call adds only SlipJay's own error text, capped at its last 1,000 characters; every allocation is a durable SlipJay attempt (an intent row written before `slipjay start --attempt`), so a failure, timeout or lost receipt is settled against SlipJay's attempt record (a finished checkout is used, never started twice; an unfinished one released, a still-running one left recorded, and the caller's error names that attempt, says whether SlipJay reports it still running or could not report its state, and tells a thread launch to retry the same request, which reconciles it, and any other caller to check it with `slipjay attempt show` since a new request starts another checkout) and a crash or restart leaves nothing stranded, because a startup sweep releases checkouts no thread is bound to or holds as an attachment and keeps those SlipJay refuses to release recorded with its reason, except that a finished thread launch whose failed preparation the thread can still retry is kept so the retry adopts it instead of allocating a second checkout (its latest run; a restart cancels a launch still preparing and nothing resumes it, so that checkout is released); one owner for SlipJay project rules. A project linked to a Forge project records it on each SlipJay workspace it allocates or adopts (`slipjay attach-project`, YS-974), so chores file there: adopting a workspace replaces or clears the record and is refused if SlipJay refuses, because a kept record would misfile later chores; an allocation that fails to record continues, since `start` already cleared it.

dispositions.upstream: Adopt canonical path grouping and require settlement or archive before unchanged-worktree cleanup. Keep SlipJay eligibility, symbolic-link refusal, archive/restore and unresolved-release guards ahead of Git removal or recreation.
requirements: a SlipJay workspace is recognised by one rule (a `.slipjay`, `.slipway` or `.pi` home's `workspaces/<name>`, under `HostProcess.HomeDirectory`; a `.jj` marker adds cleanup's reason) that cleanup and turn start both call, and recognising it never pre-empts the gates that keep a running, shared, open-session or unsettled thread's checkout; it is eligible only because its thread was settled or deleted, never for inactivity, while a git worktree keeps its inactivity clock; an eligible one is released by `slipjay retire <path> --operation <id>`, since SlipJay archives the checkout before retiring it, and the operation id derives from the thread, the workspace directory and the settlement (`unsettled` when the thread has none, else its epoch milliseconds), sanitised and capped at 128 characters, so a retry names the same operation and a resumed thread that settles again a new one, which an old attempt can never release; `git clean` is a git-worktree step only, because it would delete the ignored and untracked bytes before SlipJay archives them; whatever SlipJay refuses, cannot confirm, or answers nothing to keeps the checkout and lands in the report with that reason, and a missing or failing `slipjay` is `unavailable`, never permission to fall back to git; a turn whose SlipJay checkout is missing asks `slipjay restore --latest --path <path>` and uses the restored path, and with no archive leaves the path missing so the run fails visibly; before a turn starts on an existing one, `slipjay retire-result --path <path>` fails the run as Release unresolved (`release_unresolved`) when the record says `uncertain` or `retiring`, and lets it start on `retired`, `refused`, no record or no SlipJay at all; every `slipjay` call is bounded at 10 minutes and 4 MB of output.

dispositions.upstream: Preserve Arc commands, wake authority and removal on settle/archive while adopting upstream PR-check state and Stop settlement behavior in the same orchestrator. No upstream durable Arc owner replaces this entry.
requirements: A thread starts, checkpoints, pauses and ends its own Arc run through `t3_thread_update` action `arc_run`; delegated threads cannot, and one thread at a time owns an Arc, or each of several threads owns its own named Specs in it. Only `end` finishes a run. A completed turn with nothing set to bring the thread back gets one prompt wake naming the Arc and its role; a parked time wait counts as a next trigger until its durable timer fires. A delivered managed-task result does not end the wait while that task's child thread has a later live run, identified by its ordinal after the task's tagged result run; a same-tick or queued continuation is preserved. Completion of that child run reevaluates an active Arc parent. The watchdog uses the existing quiet/open-work thresholds to notify once when such a continuation stalls. A watchdog at 30 minutes runs as ordinary code and calls a model only for a failed or ended run, a run left unevaluated by a restart, or a stalled child. Wakes without an advancing checkpoint are capped, every turn sits under a hard ceiling, and running out makes the run `attention` with one last turn to report; attention takes priority over a stalled-child notice. Any stop of the lead pauses the run, and a client message from the owner resumes it. While a run is paused or `attention`, anything else sent to the thread queues held and waits for that message. A Spec lead's turn-end is its report to the Arc lead, and its question goes there first. A pending permission request also notifies the Arc lead without granting it authority to answer; resolved requests no longer wake it. Settling or archiving ends a run; automatic settlement skips it; a running Arc cannot be moved to another machine; starting the same Spec lead twice answers with the open one.

It covers top-level threads except Chat. A covered thread keeps working after a completed run, but not while its own background work (commands, monitors, delegated tasks, watches) will wake it; questions are answered with the away answer whichever event arrives last. Turning Away on sweeps once: waiting free-text questions are answered however old, and runs completed in the last 10 minutes continue. Agents read it through `t3_environment_read` and set it with `t3_environment_set_away` on this environment and every linked one, reached over the peer link, for which this is the only write a peer may make (`McpToolAccess.setsAway`, one hop). `workflow.unattended` stays on the wire for older clients and peers but is always false on threads; a run setup record carries Away as the run started.

requirements: a thread moves with its conversation, unpushed commits, uncommitted edits and new files; exactly one live copy exists at every point, including when the import's answer is lost (the thread stays `departing` until its deterministic import id shows up there; it is released only on an answered refusal or when the user unlinks the environment, and otherwise rechecked every 30 seconds and sent again with the same handoff id; a resent import waits for one still running there and reuses its thread and workspace; a move whose import may already have been sent, by an earlier attempt or before a restart, is never released by a failure before sending); only a full-access link carries a move; a delegated task's thread, or one with a running background command, a delegated task or a landing in flight, does not move (its waits do move, see below); in a SlipJay project the work lands in a fresh SlipJay workspace as a jj change on the moved tip; elsewhere a branch that already moved there keeps its worktree folder and a later move of it gets its own (suffixed with the handoff id); on the device composer a started thread's machine switch asks to move it to the other machine, saying why when it cannot; the first message names the source environment and thread and tells the agent to re-establish its workflow and work item; `t3_thread_import` is listed only to linked environments; `t3_thread_handoff` hides while Linked environments is off.

dispositions.upstream: Preserve account/instance aliases, pool state and credential handoff while adopting native subagent resume and provider release fixes. No upstream pooled routing replaces this behavior.
requirements: one rule (`rankAccounts` in `shared/providerPools`) places new work on an account, for a pooled turn, a scheduled or launched thread and a delegated task alike: by the pool's strategy (the member whose weekly allowance lapses soonest, weighted by plan, or the first in the pool's own order) among accounts with allowance, then accounts with no usage reading, then accounts that are out; a stored `preferredMember` is ignored. A pool can disable members, keep a reserve (a member counts as out at X% used for new work and failover, not for a running thread) and override the global switch-on-limit setting (`poolPolicy`, edited in Settings → Providers). The role resolver enumerates accounts per model and asks that rule to order and exclude them: a disabled or out account never serves while a sibling can, a model whose every account is out is skipped for the role's next, and with none left the call is refused naming the earliest return; a named account that is out yields its pool sibling offering the same model and options. A delegated task is placed like a new thread, never on its parent's account. A run failing with a usage limit that reports its reset marks its account out until then (`rememberUsageLimit`, in memory, shown as a `t3-usage-limit` window); Claude's 429s and limits with no reset are upstream errors (`api_error_429`), and a usage read decides the account. Every turn of a delegated task, follow-ups included, recovers in its own child thread through a `delegated-task.recover` outbox effect that holds the parent's delivery: a usage limit, or any failure on an account a usage read shows out, continues at once on a pool sibling (following switch-on-limit); an upstream error on a role with no other model retries after 30 seconds, up to three times. The continuation names the failed run (`manualContinuationOfRunId`), so it stays part of the same delegated task. A thread stays on its member while it has allowance and switches to the next member on a limit, with a handoff naming accounts; the chosen member's usage is refreshed before routing. The composer lamp's tooltip explains the pick (`explainPoolPick`) with each account's allowance and reset. On a new thread a click chooses the account for that thread only (the draft's selection names the member: Auto → each other account with usage left → Auto, ringed) while the model slider stays on the pool in Auto's colour; on a thread that has run it moves the thread to the next account with usage left (`thread.model-selection.set`); the lamp goes dark when every account is out. A usage card sits beside the composer, and Claude forks find threads in an account's own home. A pool's `config` holds the Claude settings its accounts share (`launchArgs`, `autoCompactWindow`, `idleCompaction`, `compactModel`, `compactOnlyWhenCold`, marked `sharedInPool` in `ClaudeSettings`): an account's effective config is the pool's valid per-field values under the account's own stored keys, resolved by `resolveProviderInstanceConfig` for the server's instance config map, the contracts compaction resolvers and the web cards; an account card stores shared fields explicitly and only "Use pool's value" removes a key. `binaryPath`, `homePath`, `customModels` and config `enabled` never inherit. Returning to a still-attached account session replaces another account's per-thread MCP credential before execution; run ownership checks stay strict.

dispositions.upstream: Adopt commit-first navigation, measured resize and cached tab titles while retaining managed navigation validation, task leases, inspected-state marking and delegated cleanup. Status no longer performs the extra title read superseded by upstream cached updates.
requirements: browser tasks (and `ui-verifier` tasks bound before T3-440) default to integrated headless Chromium; Phi requires an explicit task selection and retains its lane. Selection survives discovery, dispatch, credentials, retries and continuations. Managed credentials reach only the narrow browser endpoint: no evaluation, raw CDP or profile selection. Integrated contexts are ephemeral, task-owned and use an authenticated filtering forward proxy; only public destinations and configured `agentBrowserLoopbackAllow` host/port ranges are reachable. Every resolved address is checked, and connections use the validated IP. A forwarded request may wait up to 10 minutes on a silent allowed upstream (T3-406: a page's long request, such as YardSmith's 240 s Generate plan, gets its answer) before the proxy cuts it. Project access revocation, credential expiry and task cleanup release tabs, contexts, sockets and active recordings. Managed tools include viewport, appearance and recordings, and the device tools when agent device access is on (T3-440): the credential then carries `device`, `/mcp/browser` serves `device_*`, and `device_open`/`device_close` admit a leaf only when it drives its own browser. Phi actions report post-action URL/title; snapshot capture flags distinguish unavailable telemetry from captured-empty arrays while preserving visible-text refs.

dispositions.upstream: Adopt passive cached titles and navigation readiness without changing last-tab/profile context release, popup adoption or serialized profile clearing.
requirements: the last tab of a browser profile closes that profile's Chrome, and the shared Chromium retires five minutes after it last held a context (upstream's `idleBrowserMs`), so memory returns to the server when preview work ends. A tab owns its context from the moment it acquires it, before any start finishes, so a revoked access or a stopped start closes what it opened instead of leaking it. Since T3-571 a context start has no limit of its own: an open's start shares what is left of the open's own limit, so a slow start on a loaded machine still opens, a start that outlives it is closed when it arrives, and the open's timeout says whether the browser never started or the page never loaded.

dispositions.upstream: Use upstream Stop-state timers and replacement-action click guard in the fork dial; remove the superseded local Stop-state machine. Keep dial geometry, input marker, sound handling and remembered target machine.
requirements: model slider and reasoning dial, machine switch, docked strips, lit screen, composer sounds (keycaps click down and up); context bar always reads usage and carries the draggable compact line; machined sidebar base; Fast is set from the full model picker and shown as "Fast" under the chosen model on the slider (no Fast key, no mic button); the reasoning readout is a drum that settles with a small detent overshoot, or ratchets a row at a time across several settings, with a one-shot light sweep and per-level glass (nothing animates continuously); themes can dye the metal, and a palette theme with no device colours of its own dyes it from its sidebar colour under "Match theme". The machine switch keeps its position: a new thread without a project starts on the machine the switch was last left on (device-local, kept across restarts) instead of on the newest thread's machine, and choosing Auto balance clears that choice; a machine that no longer offers a scratch folder leaves the choice to the newest thread. A local `file:` link handed over by the OS is the exception: its fallback thread always runs on the machine running the app, because the path exists only there, and only a non-local link follows the remembered machine. The switch (lever) stays visible with load balancing instead of giving way to the strip's third option: the balancer rests the knob on its pick with a blue sparkle, moving off the pick shows an amber hand until the pick is chosen again, the tooltip names which choice is live including the still-choosing state, and knob clicks override the balancer. The automatic pick remains attached to the draft while overridden, and choosing its machine again restores Auto instead of marking both positions overridden. Opening a fresh empty draft or selecting a project requests a new automatic pick when balancing is enabled; an already open draft keeps the user's current choice. Attached files and manual workspaces pin the draft to its machine; a saved recommendation never bypasses that pin. Stored picks remain stable through connection, provider and load changes; removal from the project invalidates them. Live eligibility is checked when acquiring or applying a pick. Pending and unavailable checks show neutral indicators rather than claiming a successful choice. A sent message arrives by the chosen send motion; the default, Slide, fades the bubble in while the timeline scrolls it to the top, and that scroll starts in the frame its anchor is ready, so the arrival reads as one movement rather than a hop and then a scroll.

dispositions.upstream: Adopt upstream worker writer and passive checkpoint worker. Retire the main-thread truncate/admission handshake and microtask-yield mechanism: worker messages already yield the event loop. Keep 4000-frame checkpoint start, 10000-frame autocheckpoint backstop, bounded worker admission below 250000 frames, hard pinned-reader backpressure at that ceiling (including fully backfilled WALs that cannot restart), cancellation before posting a write, completion after posting, and checkpoint episode/timing evidence. A released episode is reported promptly; later progress can re-arm admission. Authorizer use is feature-detected (method plus all required SQLite constants); older supported Node uses non-executing EXPLAIN write opcodes, so CTE reads remain available and CTE/persistent-PRAGMA writes remain gated. No Node range changes. No new performance gain is claimed.
requirements: Claude and Codex persist streamed text, reasoning and plans at most every 400 ms per item (upstream 50 ms for text), under the web reveal's ~0.45 s lag; completion still flushes at once. Allocated event ids end in a time-ordered UUIDv7, so the unique `event_id` index grows at each stream's right edge. The passive checkpoint worker starts at 4000 WAL frames (upstream 1000), and the writer worker's autocheckpoint backstop stays at 10 000. Before an autocommit mutation or BEGIN, worker admission observes its own WAL state: below 250 000 frames it releases a pin within the configured 1 s bound, and waits again only after checkpoint progress or WAL restart, so new writes are not mistaken for checkpoint progress; at 250 000 frames the worker confirms the WAL can reset before admitting another write, including when all frames were backfilled but a reader still pins its end mark, so a reader that never lets go cannot grow the WAL indefinitely. An admission can be cancelled without executing its write; a write already posted completes before its lease is released. Held episodes report `sqlite.checkpointGate` evidence on release, cancellation and clearing (identity, reasons, start/end/peak frames, duration and held/released write counts). Writer spans retain lease, admission, BEGIN, body and COMMIT timings. The old main-thread gate, truncate handshake, unresponsive-report fallback and borrower microtask yield are superseded: admission reads the writer worker's own state, and worker RPCs already let the server event loop run. A transaction can cross the ceiling in its own write; the ceiling prevents the next mutation while its WAL remains pinned. Projection upserts for turn items, nodes and provider turns write only the columns whose values changed, because SQLite rewrites every index on a SET column even when the value is unchanged; the event log drops the unread `correlation_id` index and keeps `command_id` indexed only where it is set (migration 094).

dispositions.upstream: Adopt upstream Linux Claude launch registration and startup survivor barrier; the fork ledger still covers OpenCode, detached ACP, Pi, Codex and terminals. Their provider sets remain disjoint: upstream UUID-named Linux owner records and fork numeric group records share the directory but neither decodes or overwrites the other. requirements: OpenCode, detached ACP runtimes (Grok and Antigravity), Pi, Codex app-server sessions and terminal PTY session leaders are recorded under the state directory and forgotten when they exit; at server start, and after the desktop has stopped its servers on quit (waiting up to 3 s for a server it stopped whose stop timed out to exit, and not at all for a live server it did not start), a recorded group whose owning server is gone gets SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 2 s; a recycled pid (start time, group or command line differ) is never signalled. Codex keeps piped stdio and owns a detached POSIX group through the Effect spawner's POSIX default. Each adopter except OpenCode records its group through `trackUntilExit`, in the background, so spawning never waits on the process-table read; OpenCode keeps upstream's `OpenCodeServerLedger`, which records while the server starts and forgets when its scope closes. Where a runtime also opens a systemd scope, that scope is stopped when the process it launched exits, so a daemon a tool detached with `setsid` stops too, and a runtime that starts again within one session (Pi, for its compaction point) stops the old process's scope and starts the replacement in a fresh one (T3-223).

requirements: deterministic dev port runner for multi-instance local workflows; `migrate-dev-db` keeps stopped lead families (a stored `limitRecovery` choice never makes a family live, #113: upstream still counts it, and the 25 Oct merge restored upstream's line until SJ-5.19 removed it again) and tolerates foreign-key pruning; dev and `migrate-dev-db` default to the `.t3` of a linked git worktree or secondary jj workspace (SlipJay's, with or without a `.git` file), from its root or any nested directory, over an ambient `T3CODE_HOME`; an explicit `--home-dir` / `--base-dir` wins; `t3 pair` in such a workspace never falls back to the shared home; a SlipJay workspace directory or unreadable `.jj` where no root is recognised refuses to start rather than use the shared home. A worktree's dev server skips the startup project and thread unless `--auto-bootstrap-project-from-cwd` asks for them: started from `apps/server`, the thread took the project's default and claimed a SlipJay workspace on every fresh database. `pnpm-lock.yaml` keeps the `@pnpm/exe` entries that an older standalone pnpm writes when it switches to the pinned version, so running pnpm on such a host, as on `peach-box`, leaves no change for a landing to carry.

dispositions.upstream: Adopt imported-thread idle derivation and resumed Claude native subagent state; preserve managed child work, parent questions and round visibility.
requirements: a thread waiting on subagents shows what they are doing in its sidebar row (`Lead 1.3h`, `4 implementers`, `Lead input`), in a colour of its own; a question or approval outranks work, work outranks waiting, a lead speaks before other roles at the same status, and a subagent counts as doing whatever anything below it is doing. Sidebar rows leave out the workflow chip, which stays in the thread header and the row's hover card. Every delegated subagent the thread is waiting on sits in one panel just above the composer, leads first, then other doers, then helpers, each with status, elapsed time, model, tokens, its own Stop and a hover card; doers also show their latest message, and the panel collapses to a header when there are several. Hover shows only the subagent's latest message or progress, since the row already shows the rest. A panel row and the subagent's card in the transcript read the same: role, topic, harness logo, short model name, tokens, status and time, so the card marks where it was launched and the panel manages it; the card's own hover keeps its branch, workspace and access details. A subagent that finished since the user last wrote stays as a dimmed one-line row with its finish time; after ten seconds in view it moves into a "2 finished · 1 failed" list that opens as an accordion, as does the whole panel. Finished rows clear when the user writes, or once nothing is running and the parent has settled, and Lineage keeps them. The panel is the thread's single waiting list on web and desktop (T3-565): after the subagents come the watches (thread, Forge item, landing, pull request) and awaited commands, monitors and provider-native agents as rows of the same panel (under "Subagents" and "Watching & commands" sub-headings when both exist), a stalled child (`standing.stalled`) as an amber "No activity" row counted in the header, and the wait only the person can end (`standing.waitsOnPerson`, or an older server's watch `waitsOnPerson`) as a "You" row that stays visible when the panel is collapsed. Without `standing` the header keeps its old wording plus the extra counts. Upstream's background-work strip (the timeline footer line with Details and Stop) is no longer rendered on web/desktop: `backgroundWorkNowItem` and `BackgroundWorkStrip` are gone, `useThreadLifecycle` sends only a run's Stop to the footer, and command rows keep upstream's Details dialog (`BackgroundWorkDetails`). Mobile keeps upstream's background-work sheet and the shared `presentPendingBackgroundWork`. Live subagents also leave Lineage's live groups; a wait with no special row still shows as a generic row, so nothing is dropped. Only a pull-request watch row has its own Stop (it stops that watch); every other wait ends through the header's Stop all, which interrupts the thread's background work. Sidebar rows show Needs you and Stalled from `shell.standing` through `threadStandingAttention` in `Sidebar.logic.ts`, which `resolveThreadStatusPill` and `SidebarThreadRow` both read; a request below the thread or in a linked environment, which standing cannot see, still takes the thread out of Working and notifies. A finished subagent is shown once: one that finished before the user last had the thread open is left out (`finishedPanelSubagents`'s `seenAt`). A subagent's open request is answered from the parent's composer controls and responses go to the thread that asked; the parent's own requests come first. A request opens in the row of the thread's direct child, last in the panel, and names the asker when it came from further down; one with no row opens above the composer and names who asks.

dispositions.upstream: Adopt event-driven Stop settlement, finalized-attempt waiting and Force-stop protection for a newer follow-up, keeping pausedByParentStop, stopped cohorts, local descendant propagation and user-message-only resume.
requirements: a Stop that holds the thread's queue marks each local task whose child was queued, starting, running or waiting `pausedByParentStop`, before it disposes the completion cohort; the task settles `interrupted` with its result published. The thread's next run that starts from a person's client message sends each paused task's conversation a resume message as a follow-up attached to that new run (fresh task row and cohort, so its completion wakes the parent); a resumed task does the same for its own paused tasks, and its message releases the child's held queue as a person's would. An agent wake or scheduled run resumes nothing. A cohort disposal by Stop marks the delivery `stopped`, which leaves the task open to `delegate_task` follow-ups; `task_cancel` clears both marks and closes it. A tree walk's Stop ends a child whose run is `waiting` with no background work as `interrupted`. Linked-environment tasks are neither marked nor resumed.
